Over the last two weeks, I’ve received hundreds of emails and messages about the events in Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. 

We have all been horrified by the suffering and loss.

Many government MPs spoke about the issue in parliament this week. Our contributions reflected our different perspectives, but we were united in our belief that the priority for the Victorian Government must be our own multicultural communities.

Thousands of Palestinian and Jewish Victorians have friends or family caught up in the conflict. Many are fearful and anxious. Social media content can compound their anxiety. One-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Palestinian suffering circulate in our Muslim communities, and one-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Israeli suffering circulate in our Jewish communities.

The priority for the Victorian Labor Government, as the Premier has made clear, is to provide love and support to all Victorians who have friends or family in Israel, Gaza or the West Bank, regardless of their religion or race. The last two weeks have been incredibly tragic for some, and traumatic for most. People who have spent their lives hoping for peace have seen it ripped away again.

We have spoken with affected local residents. Our thoughts are with them. We will provide any support we can during this time of worry, suffering and grief.

PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — there has been renewed discussion about development at Preston Market, following the sale of the Tarascio family’s component to their joint venture partners, the Medich family, in August last year.

Any such development would take years to plan — and years to build, across multiple stages.

However, if anyone is interested, there is a large amount of information online about what state government planning provisions would apply. Some of the key requirements are:

— ensure the market buildings with heritage significance are substantially retained, including the large murals, and maintain a working market with a minimum floor area of 12,700 m^2 

— provide approx 1,200 dwellings, including social and affordable housing, with a discretionary maximum of 14 storeys at the northern end and 4 storeys at the southern end 

— include approx 27,500 m^2 of retail floor space, and 5,000 m^2 of office floor space 

— provide a public open space adjacent to the market with a minimum area of 2,700 m^2 and a public open space adjacent to Preston Station of approx 1,000 m^2, with the ownership of both to be transferred to Darebin Council 

— encourage a modal shift to active and public transport 

— ensure adequate car parking for the market and other uses

— encourage loading, servicing and car parking areas to be located underground 

— encourage best-practice environmentally sustainable development outcomes in line with statewide commitments to net zero emissions, and achieve an average 0.5 stars above the prevailing NatHERS requirement for each building 

— provide electric charging points for bicycles and cars 

— provide for the use of alternatives to gas 

— deliver appropriate development staging to allow continuity of market trade throughout the redevelopment of the precinct and to support the viability of business for stall holders.

Note that if any development did proceed, it would probably begin on the two sites west of the train line at St Georges/Murray and St Georges/Cramer. They have maximum heights of 13 and 8 storeys respectively.

ERIC STREET UPDATE — the two public housing walk-ups at 15–17 Eric Street have been proposed for demolition.

In the reel, I say that the Minister for Planning has given permission for demolition to proceed. To be completely accurate, a final decision hasn’t been made yet. Homes Victoria has completed the consultation and is preparing a planning application for demolition. If you have any questions or concerns, we can still follow up.

Some other points of note from reading the reports…

— The planning report says the vacant apartments are no longer suitable for housing due to their age, poor condition, fire damage, poor environmental performance and the difficulty of bringing them up to current building standards.

— The heritage report says the statement of significance in the original heritage overlay was not accurate in describing the blocks as “an unusual development of pre-cast concrete walk-up flats”. Nonetheless, it recommends the preparation of an archival-quality photographic record in accordance with Heritage Victoria’s guidelines.

— The preliminary arboricultural report assesses 24 trees within the site itself. It says the concept design may allow some trees in the central courtyard to be retained, including two mature melaleucas. Most trees on the site are exotics.

VISY UPDATE – if you are concerned about the odours from the Visy recycling plant, please sign the parliamentary petition via the link in the comments. 

BACKGROUND INFO

Visy has been producing cardboard packaging at the Radford Road site since 1959. The recycling plant opened in 1983.

There is some debate about when the odour issue started. Many people date it to roughly 2020, when Visy began recycling more water and using more household feedstock (which includes more food residue than industrial feedstock).

Bacteria in the plant’s recycled water systems produced sulphides and volatile fatty acids, which can cause strong odours.

Following complaints from residents, the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) issued a series of notices to Visy requiring the company to investigate and rectify the issue. The rectification measures included:

— introducing a bacteria control program (from 2020)
— increasing the use of fresh water for flushing (from 2021)
— switching back to industrial feedstock (from 2022)
— sealing roof vents and building gaps (2022–2025)
— extending exhaust systems and installing new stacks and fans (2021–2026).

Visy claims that the changes have resulted in a 91% reduction in measured odour units at the plant.

However, we don’t believe the reduction experienced in the community has been anywhere near that amount.

We have doorknocked all homes within 500 metres of the plant: once in 2022 and again this year.

While different people have different senses of smell, the odours remain a serious problem for many households. In 2022, we estimated that more than 200 households felt the odours were having a major negative impact on their lives. In 2026, we estimate that more than 100 households continue to be affected that way.

A local resident, Frieda De Doncker, has started a petition asking the EPA to impose further, urgent odour control requirements. We support that ask.

We are sponsoring the petition to provide further evidence about the number of households affected.

We will continue to raise the issue in parliament and with the minister.
